---
title: "Limitations and missing sources"
---

Official records survive and remain publicly accessible unevenly across institutions and periods. Search interfaces change, historical indexes can be incomplete, and older documents may no longer have linked official landing pages. A retrieval gap indicates missing coverage rather than the absence of relevant Canadian activity or documentation.

Official-language symmetry is incomplete. Some publishers provide only one accessible language version, while some historical publications are inseparably bilingual. English and French versions may also use different formulations. Bilingual pairing therefore depends on authoritative links or identifiers, and missing counterparts remain visible rather than being inferred from title similarity.

OCR and text extraction vary in quality. Image-only scans, complex parliamentary columns, damaged text, and page-by-page archives can obscure headings, dates, context, or relevant wording. Publication dates are not consistently available, especially for historical or evergreen pages; uncertain dates remain explicit. Page-modification dates are not treated as publication dates.

Institutions differ in document length, genre, publication frequency, digitization, and archival practice. These differences affect documentary visibility and the apparent distribution of institutions, families, concepts, and engagements. Visibility in the corpus is not equivalent to governmental importance, effort, or activity.

Institutional attribution identifies the official issuer or producer, not every organization or actor involved in the documented action. Document families necessarily simplify publications that may combine several functions, although multiple family assignments are allowed where several domains are substantively represented.

Concept and spatial coding depend on explicit configured wording. Contextual matching and human review reduce false positives, but implicit concepts may remain undetected, translations may use different expressions, and poor OCR may create false negatives. The absence of a confirmed concept does not prove that the underlying idea is absent from a document.

The engagement board is a curated analytical layer rather than an exhaustive inventory or a measure of intervention intensity. Combining documents under one engagement can conceal documentary variation, while separating actions requires explicit official evidence. Missing or approximate dates affect placement, and the period of an international mandate may differ from the period of Canadian participation. Chronology alone does not establish causality.

This resource supports research judgment but does not replace consultation of the linked official record before citation.
